newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba would be prepared to take Lima rebels.
newsitem.headline: Cuba would be prepared to take Lima rebels.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori said on Monday after talks with Cuban leader Fidel Castro that Cuba would be willing to grant asylum to leftist rebels holding hostages in Lima, if all parties involved including the rebels agreed to this.

Fujimori, paying an unexpected visit to Havana, told a news conference he had raised the possibility of Cuba giving asylum during his talks with President Castro on resolving the 76-day-old hostage crisis. Cuba had indicated its willingness to take in the rebels, he said.

"Cuba is willing to cooperate in the framework for this asylum, but not to participate as a mediator," said Fujimori, who arrived in Havana earlier on Monday after visiting the Dominican Republic on Sunday.
Some 20 rebels of the Marxist group Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) are holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, in Latin America's longest hostage crisis.
"I was received by President Castro with a great deal of understanding," Fujimori said. "It was a fruitful conversation."
The Peruvian leader's comments followed weeks of speculation that Cuba might be asked to play a role to end the crisis. But until now, Cuba had declined all comment on such speculation.
Fujimori said Cuba's position would be transmitted to Peruvian government officials negotiating with the rebels, who would in turn pass the message on to the rebel group.
Fujimori stressed an asylum solution involving Cuba could only be achieved if all parties formally agreed.
However in Pamplona, Spain, a spokesman for the MRTA in Europe said the MRTA rebels would not accept exile.
"We are not thinking about leaving Peru," spokesman Isaac Velasco told reporters. He was speaking before news of Cuba's position emerged.

From the start, Cuba was cited in foreign news reports as a possible mediator in the crisis, or as a place of refuge for the rebels. The MRTA is said to be inspired by Cuba's revolution but it is not known to have any links with Havana.
Havana's discretion until now and its insistence it did not want to act as a mediator appeared to reflect Castro's reluctance to be viewed as having a link with the group.

Fujimori's visit to Cuba was shrouded in secrecy until the moment he arrived and was met at Havana airport by Castro. Cuban government officials did not even confirm the Peruvian leader was coming until his plane landed.

Fujimori had been thought to be returning to Lima on Monday direct from the Dominican Republic, where he held a 3 1/2 hour meeting on Sunday with President Leonel Fernandez. He was expected to leave Havana for Lima later on Monday.

While ruling out the main demand of the rebels -- the release of 400 jailed comrades -- Fujimori has indicated he might make other concessions. He has always left the way open to asylum in another country for rebels, who seized their captives during an embassy cocktail party on Dec 17.

News reports have said Cuba, Nicaragua or a country in Eastern Europe could be potential places of asylum for the rebels. Peruvian media reported on Monday that the Dominican Republic may take six of the hostage-takers.
Castro mediated in June 1995 to secure the freedom of the brother of former Colombian president Cesar Gaviria. Some of the kidnappers and their families flew to Cuba.
Havana also intervened to help resolve a crisis in Colombia in 1980 when guerrillas of the M-19 movement seized 14 ambassadors at the Dominican Embassy residence in Bogota.
The heavily armed squad of MRTA rebels originally took hundreds of hostages but freed most of them in the first weeks, including two Cuban diplomats.
